label: Challenger Revealed Using Crack Cocaine
detail: Days before the vote, reports surface that the Republican nominee has been using crack cocaine.
assumption: Voters learn on the eve of the election that the party challenger uses a hard drug; some voters lose confidence in him, with the effect strongest among religious, older and moderate voters, and some stay home or shift to other candidates.
anachronism_note: Crack cocaine as a street drug only became widely known in the mid-1980s; in 1980 the term and its coverage did not yet exist, though freebase cocaine did.
facts_text: Newspapers across the country have given prominent coverage in the closing days of the campaign to the question of drug use by one of the leading candidates.
Editorial pages have called for a full public accounting before voters go to the polls.
nominee_news: He has been reported to have begun using crack cocaine, according to accounts published in the final days of the campaign.
Aides have neither confirmed nor denied the reports, and editors have called on him to answer questions about his health and judgment.
research_questions: How did voters respond to late-breaking personal scandals involving a major-party candidate in earlier US presidential elections?
How did turnout and vote choice shift among religious and older voters after a candidate was publicly linked to drug use?
What happened to the support of a candidate in other races when a drug scandal broke in the last week before the vote?
